listenings.text: I rebuild board decks for a living, and I only ever ask one question about a slide. Does it serve the through-line? If it does, it stays. If it does not, it goes to the appendix. That is the whole method, and it is harder than it sounds, because the slides that fail the test are usually good slides. The appendix is what makes this possible at all. Nobody can cut when cutting means losing the work. Move it to the back and the work is still there, still yours, still available when somebody asks. It is simply no longer standing between the room and the decision. And the hardest slide to cut is always the one you are proudest of. That is not a coincidence. You are proud of it because it took you three days, and three days of your work is not the same thing as three minutes of the board's attention. One more thing. A deck with no through-line makes the room do the work of finding the point, and a room that has to do that stops trying somewhere around slide six.

For years I believed that presenting in another language meant compensating. If my English was going to be simpler than my own language, then I had better use more of it, so that nobody thought the ideas underneath were simple too. It took an unkind colleague to show me what was actually happening. The extra words were not protecting the ideas, they were burying them, and the room was reading the length as uncertainty. Now I do something almost mechanical. I write the fact. Then I ask myself, out loud, so what? And whatever answers that question is the sentence that goes on the slide. The fact itself goes underneath, in small type, for anybody who wants it. The strange part, and it still surprises me, is that the sentences that survive are shorter than anything I would write in my own language. And they land harder. It turns out that a second language does not make you simpler. It just removes your ability to hide.

extra_audio.text: The growth is real, and it has bought us a risk we have not priced. What drove the quarter was the corporate portfolio. What it exposes us to is one bad season. What I need from you today is a decision on the limits.

paras: The growth this quarter is real, and it has bought the region a risk that has not yet been priced. That is the whole of this note; everything below it is evidence.

What drove the quarter was the corporate portfolio, which accounted for roughly two thirds of the eleven percent. What it cost the region was capacity in the south, where tighter underwriting absorbed more of the team than planned. What it exposes us to is a single bad climate season, at limits that were last revised in February.
It was only in September that the double counting in Argentina surfaced, and it has been corrected. The variance there is explained separately and does not change the argument of this note.

What is requested on Thursday is a decision on the exposure limits for the coming year. Market granularity, broker analysis and reserving detail are in the appendix and will not be presented unless the board asks for them.
reading.source: Board pre-read -- Commercial Directorate, circulated two days before
